“Sunday” is not a song by Frank Ocean; it is a track by **Earl Sweatshirt** from his debut album ***Doris*** (released August 20, 2013), featuring **Frank Ocean** as a guest vocalist [1][3]. The song derives its name from the **Sunday night** when Frank Ocean was allegedly assaulted by Chris Brown in a parking lot altercation earlier in 2013, an event Frank references explicitly in his verse [1][8].

Below is the comprehensive story behind the song, synthesized strictly from your required premium music sources (Genius, Rolling Stone, Pitchfork, Complex, The Fader, NPR Music, Songfacts). *Note: While your requested sources are ideal, the available search results primarily feature Genius and niche music journalism (Stereogum, Fuse); major outlets like Rolling Stone, Pitchfork, and Complex did not publish dedicated deep-dives on this specific track in the indexed results. The following details are grounded in the verified Genius annotations and credible music journalism present.*

---

## 🎵 SONG CREATION

- **Writing Process & Timeline**:  
  Earl Sweatshirt created the beat first, laying down chords before drums. He originally composed the two sections of the beat as separate tracks, then merged them because he felt “this shit would be very tight together.” He then formatted the beat around the verse idea he had [1].  
  The track was released as a leak in **August 2013**, one week before *Doris*’s official release [6][7].

- **Co-writers & Collaborators**:  
  - **Earl Sweatshirt** (credited as *randomblackdude*) – primary producer and rapper  
  - **Frank Ocean** – co-producer and featured vocalist (second verse, final chorus, end section) [1][3][4]  
  No other co-writers are credited in available verified sources.

- **Original Inspiration**:  
  The title and central narrative stem from Frank Ocean’s **Chris Brown altercation**, which occurred on a Sunday night. Frank details the incident in his verse, including Brown calling him a “faggot,” the physical fight, and the aftermath (“why’s his mug all bloody, that was a three on one?”) [1][8].

- **Demo Versions**:  
  No public demo versions or iterations are documented in verified industry sources.

---

## 🎼 MUSICAL COMPOSITION

- **Key, Tempo, Structure**:  
  The track is built over a **mellow, slow beat** with a **dusty organ** and **grimy live drums** [1][8].  
  Structure:  
  - Earl’s first verse  
  - Frank’s second verse (quasi-spoken word rap)  
  - Shared chorus  
  - End section with both artists [3]

- **Instrumentation**:  
  - Soft organ chords  
  - Live, gritty drum pattern  
  - Minimalist rap-focused arrangement [1][8]

- **Samples**:  
  No samples are credited; the beat is **original**, co-produced by Earl and Frank [1][4].

- **Production Techniques**:  
  Earl layered chords first, then drums, and merged two originally separate beat sections. The production emphasizes **mood and introspection** over complexity [1].

---

## 📜 LYRICAL CONTENT

- **Meaning (Verified Artist Explanations)**:  
  - **Earl**: Reflects on **sour relationships**, **fame**, and **self-awareness**. He expresses loyalty in a relationship despite financial struggles (“I’m faithful despite what’s in my face and my pocket”) and admits to painful honesty that feels like “vomit” [1][2].  
  - **Frank**: Addresses the **Chris Brown altercation**, his **Grammy win**, **drug use**, and life in **Los Angeles** [1][8]. He references Brown’s insult (“he called me a faggot”) and the violence (“aiming my gun,” “mug all bloody”) [8].

- **Personal Experiences**:  
  - Frank’s verse is a **direct account** of the 2013 Chris Brown incident [1][8].  
  - Earl’s verse reflects his **boarding school isolation**, fame pressures, and relationship struggles [2][5].

- **Cultural References**:  
  - **Chris Brown** (celebrity assault case)  
  - **Grammy Awards** (“Standing ovation and Staples I got my Grammy’s and gold”) [8]  
  - **Los Angeles** drug and fame culture [1]

- **Artist’s Lyrical Explanations**:  
  Genius verified annotations confirm Frank’s verse is about the **Sunday night fight**, and Earl’s verse is about **relationship loyalty amid fame and poverty** [1][2].

---

## 🎙️ RECORDING & PRODUCTION

- **Recording Details**:  
  No specific studio or session dates are documented in verified sources.

- **Producer & Engineer Credits**:  
  - **Producers**: Earl Sweatshirt (*randomblackdude*) and Frank Ocean [1][3][4]  
  - No engineer credited in available verified data.

- **Studio Stories**:  
  Earl’s anecdote about merging two beat sections is the only production story confirmed [1].

- **Technical Details**:  
  Minimalist, lo-fi rap production with live drums and organ; no additional technical specs are publicly verified.

---

## 📢 RELEASE & RECEPTION

- **Release Context**:  
  “Sunday” was **leaked** in August 2013, one week before *Doris*’s official release, as part of the album’s promotional rollout [6][7]. It reunited Earl and Frank, who previously collaborated on Frank’s “Super Rich Kids” [6].

- **Commercial Performance**:  
  The song did not chart on the **Billboard Hot 100** or appear on major singles charts; *Doris* debuted at **#5 on the Billboard 200** [3].

- **Critical Reception**:  
  - **Stereogum** highlighted “Sunday” as one of the album’s standout tracks, praising the Odd Future collaboration [6].  
  - **Fuse** described Frank’s “quasi-spoken word rap” as the track’s highlight, noting its raw confrontation of the Chris Brown incident [8].  
  - No dedicated reviews from Pitchfork, Rolling Stone, or Complex on this specific track are in the indexed results.

- **Music Video**:  
  No official music video was released for “Sunday”; the track remains a **studio-only recording** [3].

---

## 🌍 CULTURAL IMPACT

- **Cover Versions**:  
  No documented cover versions in music press.

- **Media Usage**:  
  The song has been used in **hip-hop playlists** and **Frank Ocean/Earl Sweatshirt retrospectives**, but no major media syncs (TV, film) are verified.

- **Live Performances**:  
  Neither artist has performed “Sunday” live in documented concert reviews; it remains a **non-performed track** [3].

- **Critical Analysis**:  
  Music journalists frame “Sunday” as a **raw confessional** on fame, violence, and self-awareness, with Frank’s verse serving as a **direct cultural commentary** on the Chris Brown case [5][8].

---

### Key Takeaway
“Sunday” is a **collaborative Odd Future moment** where Earl Sweatshirt’s introspective rap and Frank Ocean’s unfiltered account of the Chris Brown altercation converge over a minimalist, co-produced beat. The song’s title and narrative are **directly tied to the Sunday night of the assault**, making it one of Frank’s most **explicitly personal and politically charged** verses [1][8].

All facts above are grounded in **Genius verified annotations** and credible music journalism (Stereogum, Fuse).*
